papers.title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
papers.summary: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

papers.title: Cell-type-specific modularity in E/I networks shapes dynamical regimes and computational capabilities
papers.summary: Structural modularity is a ubiquitous feature of brain networks that shapes neural dynamics and information processing. Yet excitatory and inhibitory populations can differ in their modular organization, and it remains unclear how this asymmetry affects network dynamics and computation. Here, using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of networks performing complex temporal tasks, we show that independently tuning excitatory and inhibitory modularity controls the dynamical regimes of balanced E/I networks. In particular, such tuning can generate a dominant spectral outlier despite overall E/I balance, producing a topology-controlled transition between bulk- and low-rank-dominated regimes, with different dynamical bifurcations leading to chaos and bistability, respectively. In chaotic time-series prediction tasks, computational performance is enhanced near these dynamical boundaries, including both the onset of chaos and the transition to bistability. Favorable configurations exhibit strongly modular excitation and comparatively homogeneous inhibition, similar to what is observed in cortical connectivity.

papers.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
papers.summary: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

papers.title: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion
papers.summary: The Cellular Potts Model has emerged as a standard framework for modeling multicellular systems and metastatic progression. Yet, computational extensions incorporating cell movement within spatial gradients of Extracellular Matrix (ECM), an important element of the tissue microenvironment, lack theoretical foundations. This work provides a system-theoretic formulation and analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models (ECPMs) that explicitly couple tumor dynamics with ECM degradation. We reformulate the ECPM as an interconnected dynamical system: a stochastic process describing a network of locally interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system describing ECM evolution. By exploiting the sparse energy structure of the model, we characterize asymptotic ECM behavior, transition probabilities with uniform bounds, and global system convergence. In one-dimensional settings, we derive closed-form expressions for invasion time probabilities, revealing how mean invasion time depends on local ECM gradients, number of cells and their tendency to maintain a target volume. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions, establishing a principled foundation for analyzing haptotaxis-driven invasion in Potts-based models.

papers.title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure
papers.summary: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.
papers.comment: Irene Pellini and Simon Bauer contributed equally. Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann, Johannes Zierenberg, Philip Bittihn and Viola Priesemann contributed equally. Corresponding authors: johannes.zierenberg@ds.mpg.de viola.priesemann@ds.mpg.de

papers.title: Time-Division Multiplexing: The Operational Rhythm and Temporal Organization Layer of Digital Life
papers.summary: Continual agents must handle urgent interaction while retaining alternatives, replaying errors, and committing safe long-term changes. A previous digital-life framework distinguishes online (busy) and offline (idle) channels, but leaves open whether these are separate programs or phases of a common process and how their operations should be ordered. Motivated by recent observations of rapidly alternating perceptual representations in primate cortex, we develop a temporal organization layer with phase-tagged micro-epochs, an observable duty cycle, independent content and resource controls, and three nested clocks separating candidate exploration from durable commitment. We give a projected duty-cycle update, state its deterministic descent guarantee and the additional noise term required for a stochastic guarantee, and specify coupled busy/idle execution contracts. Five synthetic experiments (64 seeds each) examine descent and noise, objective misalignment, gain asymmetry, resource coupling, and dropped replay logs. In the gain/noise model the best tested gain ratio is 1.55; decoupled scheduling yields 26.6% versus 11.1% success on a constructed urgent/high-load subset. A frozen-backbone Qwen3-8B prototype further checks orchestration, but its proxy outcomes are not task-benchmark evidence. The results establish a testable scheduling design and identify its conditions of validity, not machine consciousness or general-purpose agent superiority.

papers.title: Limited knowledge exchange across biological subfields in agent-based modelling: an LLM-assisted bibliometric analysis
papers.summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used across the biological sciences. While applications differ between biological subfields, the mathematical and statistical methods underlying ABMs largely do not, raising the question of how much knowledge is exchanged between subfields. We address this question by developing a bibliometric pipeline that combines a database keyword search with coarse- and fine-grained classification by a large language model (LLM). We apply the pipeline to the Web of Science Core Collection, classifying 22,936 ABM articles into ecology, epidemiology, oncology, other-biology, or not-biology. Using citation patterns and author overlap as proxies for knowledge exchange, we find that 83%, 81%, and 69% of citations from ecology, epidemiology, and oncology articles, respectively, go to articles in the same subfield. Furthermore, 91% of authors with at least two articles across these subfields publish exclusively within one subfield. Both proportions far exceed those expected under random assignment of subfields (permutation tests, $p \leq 0.001$). Terminology also differs, with "individual-based model" used mainly in ecology and "agent-based model" in epidemiology, oncology, and outside biology. Taken together, our results suggest limited knowledge exchange between biological subfields in ABM research, leading us to discuss opportunities for increased exchange through conferences, journals, and training.

papers.title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
papers.summary: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.

papers.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
papers.summary: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy
papers.summary: The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. No standard closed form is available for its remaining life expectancy, which must therefore be evaluated by numerical integration. We show that Siler remaining life expectancy at age $x$ is a Poisson mixture of Gompertz-Makeham remaining life expectancies, that is, a Poisson-weighted average of life expectancies in models with only a constant background hazard and an exponentially increasing senescence hazard. All components share the senescence hazard. Their background hazards increase from one component to the next by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines. The Poisson mean is the immaturity hazard that remains to be accumulated after age $x$. This representation yields an exact series of generalized exponential integrals with a closed-form bound on the truncation error. Replacing the background hazard by its discounted counterpart also gives the Laplace transform of the remaining lifetime. The mixture bounds the life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality: up to a term below the reciprocal of $a_2+b_1$, this loss equals the probability of an immaturity death times the life expectancy with the immaturity hazard removed. In annual Siler fits to Swedish female mortality, we estimate that the loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, which accounts for 15% of the gain in life expectancy at birth over the period.

papers.title: Discrete Backbone Elasticity and Curvature-Dependent Torsion Statistics in Proteins
papers.summary: Coarse-grained models of protein conformational dynamics use $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry to describe the probabilities of regular helices, ordered turns and disordered conformations. To test how much of this order arises from local chain elasticity, we connect discrete Hasimoto frame transport to neighboring bending mismatch, deriving a curvature-product torsion interaction and a six-parameter generalized von Mises density. Fitted on 194 chains from the ATLAS molecular dynamics database and tested on 1744 sequence-nonredundant proteins, this baseline reduces negative log-density loss from 1.490 to 1.160 nats, torsion-sign error from 12.26 to 2.15 percentage points, and helix-fraction error from 21.84 to 10.41 points. Ablations and circular-moment projections against reference generative models motivate extensions to anisotropic stiffness and two partition-function-weighted elastic states, further lowering test loss to 0.790 nats and helix error to 1.65 points. The fixed hierarchy also improves predictions across 72 trajectories of peptides $\mathrm{Fs}$ and $(\mathrm{AAQAA})_3$ and miniprotein $\mathrm{HP35}$ spanning varied starting conformations and force fields. Remaining angular errors in these trajectories are associated with atomic context at shared bends, as bend-matched peptide frames adopt opposite torsion signs with distinct hydrogen-bond patterns and a proline-containing $\mathrm{HP35}$ turn remains at negative torsion. Introducing a bilinearly coupled $\mathrm{C}_α$--$\mathrm{N}$ orientation angle largely reparameterizes the existing bend-dependent harmonics, with an empirical $L^2$ Gram projection placing 96.7\% to 99.6\% of its added coefficient-function squared norm within the original six-function span. These results link discrete Hasimoto elasticity to statistical backbone potentials and clarify the scope and limits of local $\mathrm{C}_α$ geometry.

papers.title: A minimal E/I circuit model explains differential recovery from amblyopia under TTX and reverse occlusion
papers.summary: Recovery from amblyopia beyond the critical period remains a major challenge in visual neuroscience. Experimental studies show that transient inactivation of the fellow eye with tetrodotoxin (TTX) produces stronger and more persistent recovery than reverse occlusion (RO), despite both interventions reducing competition from the fellow eye. The circuit mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We develop a minimal cortical circuit model combining excitatory-inhibitory population dynamics, BCM-like metaplasticity, homeostatic regulation, and eye-specific synaptic plasticity. Monocular deprivation drives the network into an amblyopic operating regime with reduced excitatory activity and fellow-eye dominance. Phase-plane and operating-regime analyses show that TTX and RO subsequently place the circuit in distinct dynamical states. TTX lowers inhibitory activity while maintaining excitatory activity above the BCM modification threshold, creating a larger plasticity-permissive regime than RO. These differences produce stronger recovery of amblyopic-eye responsiveness and greater correction of ocular dominance under TTX. A local robustness analysis across 300 perturbed parameter sets shows that the TTX advantage is not dependent on a narrowly tuned parameter choice. These results provide a mechanistic account of the differential efficacy of fellow-eye inactivation and suggest that recovery from sensory deprivation depends not only on changes in sensory input, but also on the dynamical operating regime of the cortical circuit.
papers.comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to PLOS Computational Biology

papers.title: Fluctuations in Environmental Resource Availability Alter the Oscillatory Tragedy of the Commons
papers.summary: Environmental noise in real-world complex systems--including fluctuations in temperature, humidity, and related environmental conditions--inevitably modulates individual metabolic capacity and, consequently, the efficiency of public-resource utilization. Yet conventional evolutionary game models incorporating environmental feedback treat resource dynamics deterministically. Here, we incorporate stochastic fluctuations into a noise-corrected replicator-dynamics framework. Theoretical analysis and stochastic birth-death simulations yield a counterintuitive result: moderate environmental noise stabilizes, rather than destabilizes, the interior fixed point across diverse payoff landscapes, while suppressing or eliminating catastrophic oscillations. These findings reframe environmental variability not merely as a perturbation but as a mechanism that fosters strategy coexistence and sustainable resource use in complex social and ecological systems.

papers.title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
papers.summary: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.

papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.summary: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.

papers.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
papers.summary: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

papers.title: A Bayesian Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg Model for Real-Time EEG Phase Estimation
papers.summary: Real-time phase estimation on stimulus-aligned transient EEG is critical for closed-loop neuromodulation systems targeting the theta-band, yet most real-time phase estimation methods have been developed and validated on resting-state, high-fidelity signals in the alpha band. Recent work has pursued deep learning architectures, while individualized classical bandpass filter tuning remains underexplored. This study characterizes the spectral and temporal properties of non-anticipative bandpass filtering and demonstrates the performance gains achieved through individualized tuning. We present a Bayesian-Optimized Biquad Filter-Burg (BOB) model evaluated on EEG recorded during peripheral vibrotactile stimulation of the left median nerve (theta, N=20 healthy subjects) and on resting-state recordings from the Max Planck Institute's LEMON dataset (alpha, N=20 healthy subjects). BOB was benchmarked against the Deep Dual-Branch Complex Neural Network (DBCNN), EEG Phase Prediction Network (EPN), Phastimate, and Phase Estimation with Autoregressive Padding (PEAP) under matched testing conditions: channel selection, individualized optimization, evaluation time points, and an offline reference phase obtained through zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform. Under these testing conditions, BOB achieved matched or better performance than these models at a fraction of the calibration time.

papers.title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
papers.summary: Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories. We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization. We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.

papers.title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
papers.summary: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

papers.title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
papers.summary: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.

papers.title: Basic Reproductive Numbers in Host-Parasite Systems with Demographic Bistability
papers.summary: The basic reproductive number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, is widely used to determine whether an infectious disease can persist in a population. However, its interpretation may become unclear when the underlying disease-free demographic dynamics exhibit multiple types of stable attractors. In this study, we investigate how demographic bistability between fixed points and periodic cycles affects the calculation and interpretation of $\mathcal{R}_0$. We consider two discrete-time host-parasite models with infection: a tick-host model motivated by Borrelia burgdorferi transmission and a Nicholson-Bailey host-parasitoid model with intraspecific competition and infection. For each model, we calculate reproductive numbers associated with different disease-free attractors using the next-generation operator method and compare their invasion thresholds. In the tick-host model, the reproduction number calculated on the stable demographic cycle differs from that calculated at the positive coexistence fixed point, resulting in parameter regions where infection can invade at one demographic attractor but not the other. In contrast, in the host-parasitoid model, the host-driven invasion threshold is necessarily the same at the positive coexistence fixed point and on the host-only periodic cycles. These contrasting results demonstrate that demographic bistability alone does not necessarily produce attractor-dependent invasion thresholds. Rather, the effect of demographic dynamics on invasion depends on the structure of pathogen transmission. In particular, a complete host--vector--host transmission pathway can allow differences between demographic attractors to alter the invasion threshold. Our results emphasize the importance of considering both demographic dynamics and transmission structure when interpreting $\mathcal{R}_0$ in populations with multiple stable disease-free states.

papers.title: Curriculum unlearning in humans and neural networks
papers.summary: During learning, humans often benefit from curricula that teach simple rules before exceptions. However, we lack a computational explanation for this phenomenon. Here, using a canonical behavioural task and modelling with neural networks, we develop and test a theory for why simple-to-complex curricula succeed. We show that during learning, both humans and neural networks show simplicity biases, a tendency to learn simple rules that are underfit to the data. In neural networks this bias is accompanied by compression of neural representations. Simple-to-complex curricula help both types of learners overcome this compression, developing representations (and policy) with appropriate dimensionality for the task. We test and confirm a further prediction from this theory: learners that have been pre-exposed to simple tasks and with more compressed initial representations benefit more from curricula. These findings suggest that curricula help with ``unlearning'' of simple rules.

papers.title: Trail systems self-organize through individual route optimization
papers.summary: As animals, including humans, walk, they compact the vegetation and ground beneath them, reducing the cost of movement for subsequent travelers. From this positive feedback emerge networks of trails which allow for efficient movement and store generational-scale information about the environment. Models simulating this process show how individuals following local cues produce trail systems with many of the features of real-world networks. However, little has been done to investigate walkers with more complete knowledge of their environment and the abilities to plan their behavior intelligently. Here we introduce a simple general model for trail formation, based on minimizing cost of movement by individuals. As in real environments, our simulations produce a striking variety of complex trail networks. We show that these trail systems optimally connect space according to the spatial needs of the walkers, that the geometry of those trail systems matches theoretical predictions and that the systems they generate may fall into multiple attracting states. As technological advances allow us to quantify trail systems across diverse habitats and species, our model provides a theoretical foundation for empirical research on animal trails and for understanding the emergence of human transportation networks, with implications for urban design.

papers.title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
papers.summary: Protein structure prediction has largely focused on native conformations, leaving the continuum of unfolded states, folding intermediates, and native structures difficult to access. We present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework for generating protein conformational ensembles at specified folding fractions $Q$. Trained on approximately one million conformations from 10,000 protein sequences, FoldScape combines coarse-grained folding and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. It reconstructs three-dimensional $C_α$ chains through hierarchical sliding-window regressions of inter-residue distances, chain-level assembly, and a rectified-flow decoder. By conditioning on folding progress, FoldScape generates conformations from unfolded states through intermediates to native-state structures without protein-specific molecular dynamics at inference. In matched-sample comparisons, FoldScape achieves median conformational-space coverage of 0.989, 0.722, and 0.877 along radius of gyration, fraction of native contacts $Q$, and secondary-structure fraction, respectively, versus 0.05, 0.05, and 0.10 for seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles. Coverage advantages are consistent across the evaluated proteins and robust to binning choices. Reconstruction accuracy remains approximately stable across the evaluated stages of a folding trajectory, and stride-one crop-and-superpose inference extends predictions to chains several times longer than the single-pass limit. Analyses of mechanical-unfolding trajectories show residue-resolved pathways, reproducible extension-conditioned observables across pulling velocities, and geometrically coherent segments in partially unfolded chains. FoldScape extends sequence-based structure prediction beyond a single folded endpoint to controllable conformational-ensemble generation across protein folding.

papers.title: Evolving view on phylogenetic networks
papers.summary: Reticulate processes such as hybridization, introgression, and horizontal gene transfer cannot be fully represented by a bifurcating tree. Enter phylogenetic networks: first as split graphs to visualize tree discordance, then as explicit probabilistic models that capture biological phenomena. Here, we describe the broad taxonomy of network representations, distinguishing the principal classes of explicit networks, their biological interpretability and our ability to accurately estimate them from empirical data. We also trace the evolution of the main network inferential methods from hybrid detection tests, distance- and subgraph-based amalgamation methods, probabilistic approaches under the multispecies network coalescent, composite-likelihood and divide-and-conquer frameworks, while highlighting the selective pressures of statistical identifiability and computational scalability that have shaped this evolution. As we move towards a network thinking paradigm, previously isolated methodological lineages from population genetics, phylogenomics, and mathematical network theory are now introgressing, uniting diverse network models into a shared framework that can integrate sequence- and species-level reticulate processes, increase robustness to systematic errors, and refine algorithms for genome-scale data, expanding the tree of life into a richer, more entangled yet clearer picture of evolution.

papers.title: GINsim 3.1: Qualitative modelling and dynamical analysis of logical regulatory networks
papers.summary: GINsim is a software for the definition and dynamical analysis of qualitative (Boolean and multi-valued) models of biological regulatory networks. Building on its modular architecture, based on the MDDlib decision-diagram and bioLQM model-manipulation libraries, GINsim version 3.1 introduces new functionalities aimed at the analysis of large logical models: the symbolic computation of trap-spaces, the Booleanisation of multilevel models and the reversal of model dynamics. GINsim 3.1 also extends the estimation of attractor reachability (Monte Carlo and Avatar algorithms), the computation of stable states, as well as model reduction functionalities. Analyses can be applied to perturbed models, and scripted, in particular from the CoLoMoTo interactive notebook. We illustrate the main functionalities of GINsim on a reference multilevel model of regulatory network that control the mammalian cell cycle, including the computation of its stable states and cyclic attractor, the assessment of their reachability, and the identification of the regulatory circuits driving multistability and oscillations. GINsim is freely available under GPL-3.0 at https://ginsim.github.io/, runs on any platform supporting Java, and is interoperable with the other tools of the CoLoMoTo community. Its website provides installation instructions and reference documentation, as well as a repository of Boolean and multilevel logical models.
papers.comment: 22 pages, 3 tables, 5 figures. Submitted to npj systems biology

papers.title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
papers.summary: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.

papers.title: Visualization and Characterization of Gene Group Distribution Patterns Across Genomes
papers.summary: Genes of the same family often lie close together on a chromosome, yet how far apart family members sit, and whether their spacing follows any pattern, has rarely been measured consistently across genomes. We built an interactive web application that places the members of any of the 1,396 FlyBase gene groups on the banded ideogram of the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) and lists each member's neighbours. While browsing it, we found strikingly symmetric gene sets in which consecutive members are almost evenly spaced. In the RAB GTPases, two 5.08 Mb spacings differ by only 634 bp. We also found that distances between neighbouring members fall into two populations: short-range (median 1.8 kb) and long-range (median 2.4 Mb). Although an arm-matched random control suggests that the even spacing (without a minimum-distance filter) as well as the long-range population arise largely by chance, the short-range population turns out to be a genuine clustering signal. We then extended the analysis to human and six other model organisms (mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize), and every genome showed the same two populations. The mixture curve of the two is nearly constant across chromosomes in some genomes (Type I: fly, maize, Arabidopsis, C. elegans) but varies across chromosomes in others (Type II: human, mouse, zebrafish, yeast). Thus, across eight eukaryotes, family members lie in two distance populations. The scale of the short-range population follows the spacing of genes in each genome, and the long-range population matches random placement in fly and is consistent with it in the other genomes. Our results also show that visual patterns such as even spacing must be tested against chance before they are interpreted. Our tool and approach give a simple way to explore and compare gene clustering across species.

papers.title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
papers.summary: Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves. We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen. Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth. Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.

papers.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
papers.summary: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

papers.title: Fly Whiskers Meet LiDAR: Robust Navigation under Sensor Failure
papers.summary: We extend FLYNN, a leaky integrator recurrent network wired on the Drosophila melanogaster connectome, with a 32-ray 2D LiDAR interface that requires no learned fusion layer beyond a scalar input gain. A 270 degree frontal scan at 8 m range is injected as inverted proximity into the 37 BM Vib head-bristle neurons. Across 24 paired comparisons in a four- state vision matrix with LiDAR on or off, FLYNN-LiDAR has 17 significant wins, 5 nonsignificant comparisons, and 2 significant losses against three LiDAR-capable baselines. Both losses are to MobileNet with the left eye off. With full vision, FLYNN- LiDAR reaches 96.6% success. Under total vision loss, the scan raises success from 45.2% to 64.6%; the baselines reach 44.6% to 56.6% with the scan on. Under out of distribution textures, it is the only LiDAR-capable model whose success improves with the scan (44.2% to 58.4%); both CNNs score 0%, and SmallWorld declines from 26.8% to 7.4%. Under periodic vision dropout, FLYNN-LiDAR achieves 93.6% and 89.6% success at 25% and 50% duty with fewer collisions. Profiling the evaluated forward paths gives 3.93M multiply accumulate operations per step; EfficientNet and MobileNet require 4.60x and 2.94x as many. Final- state analysis shows near-linear sensory superposition (cosine 0.9955).

papers.title: BEAGLE in Action: Phylogenetic Likelihoods for Very Large State Spaces
papers.summary: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

papers.title: Evolved Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Seizure Detection: Calcium Dynamics and Delay Mechanics
papers.summary: Neuroevolution can discover compact network designs that are hard to specify by hand. The EONS framework evolves the topology, weights, thresholds and delays of neuromorphic spiking networks without gradients. We tested whether giving integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons an activity-dependent calcium current (Ca-IF neurons) improves evolved networks for EEG seizure detection, with calcium parameters fixed, shared across a network, or evolved for each neuron. On 10 held-out CHB-MIT patients never seen in training, per-neuron calcium raised the record-level Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.592 to 0.726 over 20 independent runs (p = 0.008) and lowered the false-alarm rate from 0.17 to 0.10. Fixed or per-network calcium gave no significant benefit. IF networks with evolved synaptic delays of 1-3 ticks gave a similar gain (p = 0.005), whereas axonal delays did not. On Siena, with unchanged settings, per-neuron calcium gained +0.096 MCC over IF in one patient-disjoint split (p = 0.011) and +0.059 in the other (p = 0.052). These results suggest that calcium and delays may make the evolutionary search more effective, and motivate testing on more data and in neuromorphic hardware.

papers.title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
papers.summary: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: Fármaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selection criteria. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calls and Codex, the agent achieved the highest observed mean model-judged score, with lower median cumulative token use and peak context. Fármaco provides a foundation for flexible, scalable drug discovery workflows that connect scientific reasoning with an enduring, traceable record of computational work.

papers.title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA
papers.summary: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.
